title: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025
author: New York State Bar Association President's Committee on Access to Justice

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source acknowledges AI-driven task reallocation and increased lawyer capacity, but shifts the central concern away from law-firm leverage, revenue and apprenticeship toward the access-to-justice capacity crisis. It frames efficiency primarily as a means to expand civil legal assistance rather than evidence of structural contraction in law firms.
qs: In a country where 92% of civil legal needs go unmet, the legal profession does not face an employment crisis.
AI can handle the repetitive and standardized tasks that now consume attorneys’ time, freeing us to focus on the parts of practice that require judgment, empathy, and advocacy.

st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source presents supervised internal assistance, a proposed sandbox for direct help to self-represented litigants, and autonomous courtroom participation as a future possibility. It does not assess whether GenAI caused rising self-representation, improved litigant outcomes, or shifted screening and verification costs to courts and opponents.
qs: If properly used, within this role GenAI acts as an internal legal assistant to the lawyer or other advocate who maintains the ultimate responsibility for any given task.

Association approved a committee to establish a GenAI regulatory sandbox with the goal of improving access to justice; if implemented, this would use GenAI to assist pro se litigants to interact with the judicial system across a wide range of subject matters, without the direct intervention of a lawyer or legal services provider.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI may assist legal work only while human professional responsibility, verification, confidentiality and security safeguards remain intact. It materially extends that proposition by operationalising it through a sample organisational policy covering permitted uses, personnel, protected information and periodic review, although it does not address competing court-specific disclosure or certification regimes.
qs: Staﬀ are cautioned to verify the accuracy and reliability of information obtained via AI-enhanced            search engines.

st.t: AI governance: Literacy and benchmarking build capacity
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s governance-and-capacity framing and materially develops it with respondent evidence on demand for practical training, alongside concrete privacy concerns arising from reliance on general-purpose public tools. It also presents service expansion and back-office gains as opportunities, while not claiming demonstrated reduction of the justice gap.
qs: •     Training Needs: Two-thirds of respondents expressed interest in AI training, with a          preference for flexible, on-demand formats.
This trend raises concerns about data privacy and the use          of public tools without enterprise safeguards.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The report accepts that technological affordability alone is insufficient and materially extends the cluster’s provider-augmentation pathway with targeted funding, shared infrastructure, safeguards, staged deployment and human fallback. Its practical examples and access claims remain largely prospective rather than quantified evidence of improved remedies.
qs: Yet, its success hinges on more than technological capability—it requires collaboration, robust safeguards, and a commitment to equity.
Without targeted funding and shared infrastructure, legal services organizations risk diverging into a two- tiered system where some scale exponentially while others fall behind.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: The source accepts AI as augmenting legal-aid lawyers and expanding bounded consumer access rather than simply replacing professional representation. It materially develops the proposition by prescribing well-scoped information tools, shared vetted infrastructure, co-development and targeted investment, while acknowledging reliability, confidentiality and unequal implementation capacity.
qs: AI can handle the repetitive and standardized tasks that now consume attorneys’ time, freeing us to focus on the parts of practice that require judgment, empathy, and advocacy.
Where to Start  A natural place to start with AI in the legal aid community is to leverage it for well-scoped use cases that allow us to scale legal information that already exists.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI must remain supervised and subject to verification, confidentiality controls and human accountability. It materially develops that position through a phased implementation framework: governance before deployment, approved-tool classifications, controlled internal pilots, training, audit trails, mandatory sign-off, secure infrastructure and delayed direct-to-client use.
qs: To do that, the following principles should guide every step:                                                    9 ^LArtificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025     •   Lead with Policy and Governance, Not Experimentation        Before deploying tools, organizations should adopt plain-language AI policies that define        permitted uses, prohibited practices, and accountability measures.
Human Review & Auditability                  ▪ Implement reviewer checklists, mandatory sign-off, and prompt/output                       logging.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s central balance: AI can expand legal-aid capacity, but direct public use shifts reliability and verification risks to vulnerable users. It materially extends that proposition with a phased implementation model—governance and bounded internal pilots first, followed by narrowly scoped client-facing tools only after evaluation and with human escalation—while also addressing training, infrastructure, independent testing and equity safeguards.
qs: On the other side is a set of maturing AI capabilities that, if deployed thoughtfully, can expand capacity, sharpen quality, and modernize systems.
•   Sequence client-facing tools: Only after governance and evaluation are working—and        only for narrow tasks with human escalation.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core supervised-copilot framing and materially extends it with a 2025 legal-services survey and a phased access-to-justice deployment roadmap. It prioritizes low-risk internal workflows, secure and grounded tools, mandatory human verification, training, evaluation and delayed, narrowly scoped client-facing use, while highlighting accuracy, confidentiality, equity and digital-exclusion risks.
qs: For lawyers, AI is best understood as a first-pass collaborator.
That pairing— grounded output + human verification—is the spine of responsible use.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The report accepts that AI can expand legal help but that uptake alone is insufficient. It materially develops the cluster’s proposition with statewide evidence showing interest exceeds actual use, plus a staged pathway requiring governance, evaluation, supervision and shared investment before client-facing expansion.
qs: In the statewide survey of legal aid professionals, nearly nine in ten reported they were either not using AI or using it only slightly in their work, yet about half said they were moderately or more motivated to use it, and nearly two-thirds believed their organizations were open to AI.

Taken together, they point to a practical path: start where value is high and risk is low, upskill the large “curious-but-not-confident” middle, engineer trust with                                                  25 ^LArtificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025  visible guardrails, and build toward carefully-supervised client-facing uses only when governance, data, and evaluation are in place.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that responsible legal-AI adoption requires active professional governance and extends it with a concrete implementation framework: pre-deployment policies, staged internal pilots, audit trails, authoritative grounding, mandatory human verification, training and equity safeguards. Its survey also grounds this framework in a documented gap between interest and institutional capacity.
qs: To do that, the following principles should guide every step:                                                    9 ^LArtificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025     •   Lead with Policy and Governance, Not Experimentation        Before deploying tools, organizations should adopt plain-language AI policies that define        permitted uses, prohibited practices, and accountability measures.
That means enterprise-grade tools with zero        data retention, retrieval-augmented grounding to authoritative sources, mandatory human        verification, and documented ethics checks.

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: The source accepts selective delegation as the central issue and reinforces the distinction between expanding use and demonstrated quality. It materially extends the cluster by framing delegation boundaries as a collective, client-centered access-to-justice question covering both represented clients and people denied service for lack of resources.
qs: From my perspective, the fundamental question that needs to be addressed is what aspects of the practice of law will we be willing to delegate to GenAI.
In answering these questions, it will be necessary to keep our clients – both those who we represent and those we turn away due to lack of resources – front and center.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-supervised, selective-deployment proposition and materially extends it with a phased civil-legal-aid implementation framework: governed internal pilots, defined reviewers and metrics, authoritative-source grounding, mandatory verification, and delayed, narrow client-facing deployment. It also adds equity safeguards and cautions that deployment reach is not evidence of improved legal outcomes.
qs: Wrap new ideas in a one-page Pilot Intake: use case, data sensitivity, grounding corpus, reviewer, success metrics, review date (30–60 days).
That means enterprise-grade tools with zero        data retention, retrieval-augmented grounding to authoritative sources, mandatory human        verification, and documented ethics checks.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s principal proposition by treating adoption as a change-management and governance problem requiring training, approved tools, phased deployment and human verification. It presents its survey as a policy baseline rather than evidence of investment returns or improved legal outcomes; its access-to-justice benefits remain predictions rather than demonstrated effects.
qs: This is the first field-wide reading designed to serve as a baseline for policy, training, and pilot design.

It requires mandatory training, restricts use to approved platforms, prohibits the entry of confidential or case-related information into public AI systems, and mandates human review of all AI-generated work product.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal education must develop AI competence alongside traditional legal skills. It favors curriculum-wide integration rather than isolated electives and adds an access-to-justice rationale, but does not address the cluster’s central disputes over timing, restrictions, assessment design or evidence of educational effectiveness.
qs: Law schools must treat AI as they once treated legal writing or research—as fundamental.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI is limited to assistive uses, users retain accountability and human judgment, outputs require independent verification, sensitive data is barred from public models, and approved tools and training govern use. It supplies a concrete UCS policy example but does not materially extend the cluster’s broader lifecycle, disclosure or effectiveness analysis.
qs: At the same time, it warns that generative AI systems can produce inaccurate, fabricated, biased, or offensive content and are unsuitable for legal research or legal writing without independent verification.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI is an assistive tool, users remain accountable, and legal outputs require independent human verification. Its approved-tool, training, confidentiality and review safeguards also align with the cluster’s organisational-governance framework; its discussion of provider liability and light-touch regulation is supplementary rather than contrary.
qs: At the same time, it warns that generative AI systems can produce inaccurate, fabricated, biased, or offensive content and are unsuitable for legal research or legal writing without independent verification.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source supports the distinction between mere exposure and professional readiness by arguing that foundational AI education must teach students not only to use tools but also to critique, regulate and improve them. Its broader access-to-justice and UPL proposals fall outside the cluster’s central judgment-development proposition, and it supplies little evidence about durable competence or independent mastery.
qs: Law schools must treat AI as they once treated legal writing or research—as fundamental.
Students should graduate not only knowing how to use AI, but how to critique it, regulate it, and improve it.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central tension: AI could expand legal assistance for people who lack lawyers, but delegation, privacy, ethics, reliability and the information–advice boundary require safeguards and deliberate governance. Its stronger calls for direct consumer access and fundamental UPL reform fit within the cluster’s documented range of reform proposals rather than displacing the cluster’s framing.
qs: In answering these questions, it will be necessary to keep our clients – both those who we represent and those we turn away due to lack of resources – front and center.
With clear disclaimers, built-in ethical safeguards, and up-to-date legal data, we can empower people to solve their own legal problems.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s copilot framing: AI can enhance productivity, but attorney responsibility, rigorous verification and governance remain essential. It likewise favours selective, lower-risk staff-facing pilots and warns that probabilistic errors are especially dangerous for users unable to assess outputs; it does not demonstrate consistent quality gains or resolution of verification costs.
qs: Attorneys must ensure that all work product is their own original work and that it is rigorously reviewed to ensure accuracy.
The susceptibility of hallucinations or miscalculations can be dangerous if relied upon by individuals without the legal expertise to assess AI outputs.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between useful AI assistance and legitimate judicial authority. Its policy treats AI as a productivity tool rather than a substitute for human judgment, retains judicial accountability, and requires verification and review. It contributes deployment safeguards but does not independently examine consent, challenge rights or whether technical accuracy could legitimate autonomous adjudication.
qs: The policy also affirms that existing ethical rules governing judges and court employees continue to apply, including judicial responsibility for decision-making and prohibitions on bias or improper disclosure.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that AI can redistribute legal work and expand capacity without wholesale lawyer replacement, while making scaled and client-facing deployment conditional on human verification, governance, evaluation and equity safeguards. Its focus is access to justice rather than provider bargaining or pricing, so it supports only part of the broader operating-model proposition.
qs: AI as a Force Multiplier  AI is not going to replace lawyers—but it is going to redefine what lawyers do, and how much they can do.
•   Sequence Client-Facing Tools Carefully        Direct-to-client AI should come later, and only after governance, training, and evaluation        systems are proven.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source strongly endorses the cluster’s core framing: AI should support rather than replace human judgment, with mandatory review, verification, governance, training and confidentiality controls. Its phased approach—internal pilots before client-facing deployment—reinforces supervised adoption; more autonomous possibilities appear only as unresolved testimony, not the report’s recommendation.
qs: Like the framework proposed here, the courts’ policy emphasizes AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for human judgment.
Human Review & Auditability                  ▪ Implement reviewer checklists, mandatory sign-off, and prompt/output                       logging.

kp.k: Survey establishes limited adoption despite widespread awareness
kp.d: The report, approved by NYSBA’s House of Delegates on January 16, 2026, combines a New York legal services survey with May 21, 2025 hearing testimony. The survey received 206 responses from 715 individuals contacted, a 28.8% response rate. It reports fieldwork from February 3 to April 9, 2025, described in the document as 75 days. Reported work integration was 52.9% not at all, 35.4% slightly, 10.7% moderately, 0.97% very, and 0% extremely. These are respondent-reported adoption findings rather than measurements of productivity or client outcomes.
qs: Number of responses: 206
Response rate: 28.8%
OVER 88% do not use AI or use it only slightly in their work.
AI is largely conceptual, recognized in theory but not yet embedded in routine practice.

kp.k: Current applications enhance existing work rather than transform delivery
kp.d: Survey respondents using AI concentrated on research, writing and editing, brainstorming, forms automation, and administration. The New York slides report research at 57.0%, writing and editing at 41.9%, brainstorming and ideation at 29.3%, forms automation at 28%, and administrative tasks at 22.2% among the group described as using AI. ChatGPT predominated, legal-specific tools had very low adoption, and 36.9% had not used generative AI tools. The report interprets these patterns as early productivity enhancement and identifies data analysis as a promising underused application.
qs: These use cases highlight AI’s role as a productivity enhancer rather than a transformative tool—at least for now.
Among those who do, ChatGPT is by far the most commonly used, while legal-specific products show very low adoption.
Initial interest in AI is focused on efficiency, not direct services.

kp.k: Accuracy, confidentiality and competence constrain adoption
kp.d: The New York survey reports inaccurate results as the leading concern at 66.67%, followed by ethical implications at 53%, data privacy and security at 51%, confidentiality at 51%, bias at 33%, and lack of knowledge and skills at 29%; 3.4% wrote in environmental impact. Some 66% wanted training, preferring on-demand support, with AI basics, ethics and hands-on tool training each requested by approximately 61%. Nearly two-thirds perceived their employers as moderately or more open to AI. The report recommends asynchronous foundations followed by role-specific clinics and office hours.
qs: Top concern = Inaccurate results (66.67%)
66% of respondents want training
The most requested topics—AI fundamentals, ethics, and hands-on tool training—were nearly equally prioritized, each cited by approximately 61% of respondents.
Nearly 2/3 think their employer is moderately or more open to using AI.

kp.k: Governance should precede phased deployment
kp.d: The committee recommends plain-language policies, approved-tool lists, accountability and training before deployment. Internal applications with established human review should precede narrow client-facing tools. Its proposed pilot process specifies the use case, data sensitivity, grounding corpus, reviewer, success metrics and a 30–60-day review date. Recommended metrics include hours saved, cycle time, error rates, staff satisfaction, first-review acceptance and distribution of benefits across geography, language, practice area and accessibility needs. These are implementation recommendations, not reported pilot results.
qs: Lead with Policy and Governance, Not Experimentation
Before deploying tools, organizations should adopt plain-language AI policies that define permitted uses, prohibited practices, and accountability measures.
Before launch, define baselines and success metrics: hours saved, cycle-time reduction, error rates, staff satisfaction, and percent of outputs accepted on first review.
Only after Steps 1–5 are stable should organizations explore client-facing tools for narrow, high-volume, high-burden tasks

kp.k: Verification remains essential despite grounding and private tools
kp.d: The report advocates private or enterprise environments with zero data retention, tenant isolation and organization-level sign-in, alongside retrieval grounding in vetted authorities, inline citations, reviewer sign-off, logging, redaction and ethics checks. Randal Jeffrey expressly cautions that retrieval-augmented generation does not guarantee accurate answers, especially for nuanced questions. The report therefore positions AI as an assistant whose output must be checked, not an independent legal authority.
qs: Treat AI as a drafting and synthesis assistant, not a final authority.
Require inline citations and link-back verification so reviewers can quickly confirm accuracy.
Implement reviewer checklists, mandatory sign-off, and prompt/output logging.
But even with RAG, the quality of the information is not guaranteed, especially in response to nuanced or highly specific questions, and any such chat-bots must be fine-tuned and vetted.

kp.k: Reported operational gains support staff-facing deployment
kp.d: The report recounts Legal Services NYC’s use of a private LLM for knowledge management, summaries and semantic retrieval, alongside finance, grant-reporting and data-analysis applications. Reported benefits include reduced overtime in accounts payable and receivable, easier organizational knowledge sharing, and analysis of poverty distributions and legal need. These are practitioner accounts rather than quantified comparative studies. Alexander Horwitz’s testimony is summarized as rejecting direct client-facing deployment for now because of reliability, explainability and the loss of nuanced human care.
qs: Finance departments use AI to reduce overtime in accounts payable/receivable and grant reporting.
Data teams use AI to analyze poverty distributions and connect geography to legal need.
Each of these wins saves time, improves quality, and does not expose clients to unvetted outputs.
Deliberate decision not to deploy AI in anything that touches clients directly

kp.k: Capacity claims favor augmentation, not staffing replacement
kp.d: The committee frames AI as increasing legal aid capacity and freeing advocates for judgment, empathy and complex work. Its testimony summary attributes a potential 2–3× effectiveness gain to Scott Reents, while Sateesh Nori asserts that one lawyer can do the work of five. These are speaker claims, not findings established by the New York survey. The committee explicitly rejects funding narratives that treat automation as grounds for reducing staff and predicts that responsible adopters will serve more people than non-adopters.
qs: AI allows one lawyer to do the work of five.
Resist “do more with less staff” narratives.
Use metrics to show that AI reduces drudgery, improves quality, and expands reach—but does not replace the human relationships at the heart of justice.
AI will not replace lawyers. But lawyers and legal services organizations that learn to harness AI responsibly will out-serve those that do not.

kp.k: Justice-gap urgency motivates adoption without proving its impact
kp.d: Lisa Colpoys cites the Legal Services Corporation’s 2022 Justice Gap Study as finding that low-income Americans received insufficient or no help for 92% of civil legal problems, and states that legal aid turns away half of those seeking help because of capacity limits. Witnesses use this unmet need to justify experimentation and expanded capacity. The report’s forecasts that AI could reduce burnout, improve court administration and extend assistance remain conditional expectations rather than measured closure of the justice gap.
qs: The Legal Services Corporation’s most recent Justice Gap Study in 2022, found that “[l]ow-income Americans did not receive any or enough legal help for 92% of their civil legal problems.”
legal aid organizations turn away half of them because they do not have sufficient capacity.
It will free advocates to practice at the top of their license, reduce burnout, and extend help to people who would otherwise get none.

kp.k: Direct client tools expose tension between access and care
kp.d: The report contrasts proponents’ argument that withholding self-help tools perpetuates inequity with practitioners’ concern that seemingly simple legal questions conceal needs involving safety, transport, childcare or health. Its recommended resolution is later, carefully supervised client-facing deployment with grounding, disclaimers, human escalation and hand-offs. The report also notes Legal Services NYC’s high-volume hotline—approximately 120,000 calls annually, about 60,000 answered—as illustrating the difficulty of monitoring interaction quality at scale.
qs: Proponents argue that because most people will never get a lawyer, withholding well-designed tools perpetuates inequity.
Today’s AI can answer the explicit question; it struggles to sense what’s unsaid.
client-facing AI should come later, not first, and only with strong governance, transparent grounding, clear disclaimers, escalation paths, and supervised hand-offs to humans.

kp.k: Case studies illustrate reach, not uniform outcome evidence
kp.d: In July 2025 written testimony, Paladin’s Kristen Sonday reports a Tennessee expungement system generating draft petitions from anonymized records for attorney review; one clinic cleared 324 charges for 98 people in one day. She also describes California Innocence Project document review using CoCounsel, North Carolina’s LIA portal receiving over 95,000 views within months, and Housing Court Answers’ separate staff and tenant tools. These are attributed implementation accounts; portal views and a clinic’s throughput are not presented as controlled measures of legal accuracy or causal improvements in outcomes.
qs: the AI tool was able to produce a draft petition for review and submission by the team’s attorneys.
Legal Aid Society cleared 324 charges for 98 people in one day
In just a few months, the AI-powered portal had received over 95,000 views and helped thousands of individuals.
Together, they suggest a future where AI doesn't replace legal professionals, but rather increases their capacity

kp.k: Witnesses differ over unauthorized-practice reform
kp.d: Sateesh Nori advocates abolishing or fundamentally reforming unauthorized-practice restrictions in favor of risk-based, evidence-informed regulation focused on results, and making safeguarded tools directly available to consumers. Randal Jeffrey identifies UPL as the primary barrier to freestanding legal AI, while emphasizing the unclear boundary between legal information and individualized advice. Sam Harden favors light-touch regulation but opposes state bars regulating AI providers. The committee adopts a more incremental position: dialogue and cautious examination of rules while protecting consumers, rather than endorsing wholesale abolition.
qs: it is time to abolish or fundamentally reform UPL laws as they currently exist.
We need a new framework—one that is risk-based, evidence-informed, and focused on outcomes.

The dividing line between legal information that can be freely provided and legal advice that involves the application of the law to the facts of an individual’s circumstances, of course, is not a clear one.
Begin with dialogue and incremental steps rather than sweeping changes, ensuring that any adjustments prioritize client safety and public trust.

kp.k: Autonomous legal work remains a prospective, contested possibility
kp.d: Jeffrey distinguishes internal assistants, external assistants and freestanding agents delivering services without attorney involvement. He raises, rather than resolves, questions about delegation ranging from intake and case explanations to drafting, filing, correspondence and strategy, and speculates about eventual courtroom participation. Harden separately proposes tool-using agents that retrieve case information, prepare medical-record requests for lawyer approval, or calendar hearings from filings. These examples describe plausible or envisioned workflows, not established deployments documented by the survey.
qs: the fundamental question that needs to be addressed is what aspects of the practice of law will we be willing to delegate to GenAI.
For me, freestanding GenAI means the provision of legal services without attorney involvement, either as a program of a legal services organization or as a separately managed application.
GenAI handling every aspect of a matter – drafting and filing documents, sending letters, corresponding via mail, and even making strategy decisions
A plausible scenario based on current AI capabilities:

kp.k: Courts need independent evaluation, not vendor assurances
kp.d: NCSC witnesses Aubrie Souza and Zachary Zarnow warn that unrepresented court users may be unable to assess authoritative-looking but erroneous answers, making accuracy, fairness, transparency and human oversight essential. They recommend internal court operations, content management, preliminary plain-language rewrites and expert-led prototyping before public deployment. They also warn that cheap initial pricing may become financially unsustainable. Separately, the report attributes to Reents a concern that faster filings could overwhelm adjudicative capacity and that speed can disadvantage tenants when delay benefits them.
qs: Unlike expert staff, people without lawyers cannot always discern whether AI-generated information is accurate, complete, or relevant.
Just because a vendor claims a tool can do something doesn’t mean that it can. Just because a tool can do something doesn’t mean that it is actually helpful.
If courts grow increasingly reliant on third-party providers, there is a real risk that future pricing models could become prohibitive.
speed may harm litigants in some contexts (e.g., housing cases where time can benefit tenants).

kp.k: Court policy preserves human accountability and confidentiality
kp.d: The report summarizes the New York State Unified Court System’s Interim AI Policy as applying to judges and nonjudicial personnel, including court work performed on personal devices. It requires approved tools, training before use and review of generated content, and prohibits entering confidential, privileged, personally identifiable or case-related information into public models. These are described as existing court-system requirements, distinct from the committee’s recommendations and the illustrative organizational policies annexed to the report.
qs: all users remain fully accountable for any work product produced with AI assistance.
UCS users may only use AI tools approved by the Division of Technology and Court Research and must complete required AI training before use.
Confidential, privileged, personally identifiable, or case-related information may not be entered into public-model AI systems under any circumstances
All AI-generated content must be thoroughly reviewed to ensure accuracy and to avoid bias or inappropriate material.

kp.k: Funding and shared infrastructure determine equitable adoption
kp.d: Colpoys, Cox and Sonday warn that legal aid organizations may lack the budgets and technical expertise needed to evaluate, implement and maintain AI, creating gaps both among nonprofits and between legal aid and commercial practice. Sonday recommends shared vetted knowledge bases, reusable blueprints, co-development and public-private investment. Cox emphasizes inventories, tagging, taxonomies, retention rules and usage rights for existing organizational documents. These recommendations contrast with Nori’s optimistic assertion that affordable and open-source models can bring the marginal cost of serving another client close to zero.
qs: AI systems are often expensive, and legal aid organizations frequently lack the budget and in-house technical expertise to evaluate and implement them.
Without targeted investment and public-private partnerships, we risk a two-tiered system
making it easier for LSOs everywhere to integrate with shared tools, vetted knowledge bases, and pre-trained models.
The marginal cost of serving an additional client approaches zero.

kp.k: Training requires institutional support and changes to legal education
kp.d: Colpoys describes the Lawyers Trust Fund of Illinois initiative, launched in September 2024, as supporting rather than replacing legal aid professionals through webinars, discussion groups, weekly office hours, peer groups of 6–10 people, a resource library and one-time project funding. Its separate October 3–22, 2024 Illinois survey had 376 responses and a 23.33% response rate, with approximately 90% reporting no or slight work use. Nori calls for AI literacy throughout doctrinal courses, clinics and bar preparation, including the ability to critique and regulate tools rather than merely operate them.
qs: the intent of this initiative is not to replace legal aid professionals with technology, but instead to support and supplement their work
They also need time and space to experiment, to learn how to use AI technology, and to integrate AI tools into their daily work.
Peer learning groups of 6-10 people from different organizations are evaluating specific use cases for AI, testing AI tools, and developing best practices.
Students should graduate not only knowing how to use AI, but how to critique it, regulate it, and improve it.

kp.k: Accessibility requires human alternatives and inclusive design
kp.d: The committee recommends that AI never become the only route to legal assistance, retaining hotlines, clinics, paper forms and in-person support alongside multilingual and assistive technology access. It also reports a separate New York City Bar disability analysis arguing that non-inclusive data and aggregate statistical approaches can obscure individualized discrimination. That external report recommends disability participation throughout development, accessibility benchmarks, community-led testing, accountability and human alternatives equivalent in convenience, cost and timeliness.
qs: Do not make AI the only way to get help.
Pair tools with hotlines, clinics, paper forms, and in-person support.
current AI development frequently excludes, misrepresents, or disadvantages disabled individuals.
Human alternatives should be equivalent in convenience, cost and timeliness.

kp.k: Vendor claims and model demonstrations require careful attribution
kp.d: Jeff Cox, speaking as a vLex marketing director and legal aid board chair, claims that authoritative-source grounding and zero-retention agreements address hallucination and confidentiality concerns; these are vendor-affiliated assertions, not independent findings. Harden reports that his 2024 survey rated one Google Bard legal response 3.11 out of 5 for helpfulness and 3.56 for actionable next steps, then qualitatively praises a later Gemini Deep Research answer to the same question. His example does not establish a general legal-accuracy rate, and he separately warns that AI can produce mistakes at scale and that provider liability remains unsettled.
qs: we've tackled the hallucination problem through an approach that grounds all AI responses in authoritative legal sources, with direct links to primary law that attorneys can verify.
survey takers rated Bard’s response as 3.11 out of 5 for helpfulness, and at a 3.56 out of 5 for giving actionable next steps.
AI can be wrong at a far greater speed and scale
Currently this is an unsettled area of law.

kp.k: Environmental impacts qualify the efficiency case
kp.d: The report’s environmental section cites external estimates rather than measuring legal aid’s own footprint: an IEA projection of global data-center electricity demand reaching 945 TWh by 2030, an estimate that GPT-3 training could directly evaporate 700,000 liters of freshwater, and a projection of up to 5 million metric tons of generative-AI e-waste by 2030. It recommends awareness, feasible questions about energy and hardware practices, and advocacy for greener standards, rather than burdensome vendor checklists for resource-constrained nonprofits.
qs: Global electricity demand from data centers is set to more than double to 945 TWh by 2030
training the GPT-3 language model in Microsoft’s state-of-the-art U.S. data centers can directly evaporate 700,000 liters of clean freshwater
Generative AI could account for up to 5 million metric tons of e-waste by 2030

this report encourages organizations to stay informed, ask basic questions about energy sourcing and lifecycle practices when feasible, and advocate for greener standards in the broader technology ecosystem.

kp.k: Report production itself used AI-assisted synthesis
kp.d: The authors disclose using Microsoft Copilot with structured prompts to review and synthesize supplied testimony and survey data, while retaining human responsibility for organization and drafting choices. They state that recommendations came exclusively from provided materials and that internet-based research was used only for the environmental discussion. This disclosure distinguishes the report’s synthesized recommendations and testimony summaries from the underlying survey findings and witnesses’ own written submissions.
qs: The drafting process utilized structured prompts to guide Copilot’s analysis and synthesis of information.
Copilot’s role was focused on reviewing and interpreting the source materials provided, which included testimony and survey data collected for this project.
All recommendations and next steps outlined in this report were synthesized exclusively from the provided source materials.
Human oversight was maintained throughout the process to ensure accuracy, context, and alignment with organizational goals.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Committee finds that AI was primarily a lightly adopted productivity aid in New York legal services in early 2025, rather than an embedded transformation of practice.
pts.d: The report's survey records 52.9% reporting no work integration, 35.4% slight integration, 10.7% moderate integration, approximately 0.97% very integrated, and none extremely integrated. Current applications concentrate on research, writing, brainstorming, forms and administration. ChatGPT predominates among generative AI users, while legal-specific tools have little uptake. The Committee interprets the gap between interest and use as a capacity, training and governance challenge.

pts.k: The Committee predicts responsible AI adoption will expand service capacity, reduce burnout and improve court operations without replacing lawyers.
pts.d: The report's central forecast is augmentation: automation and first-pass assistance free advocates for judgment-intensive work and enable more people to receive help. It also predicts that responsible adopters will serve clients more effectively than non-adopters. These are conditional strategic conclusions from the survey and testimony, not measured sector-wide outcomes or employment forecasts.

pts.k: Practitioners offer different quantitative estimates of AI's potential to multiply lawyers' capacity and lower delivery costs.
pts.d: The report's account of Scott Reents's testimony attributes to him a potential two- to threefold effectiveness gain and lower legal-service costs. Sateesh Nori claims one lawyer can do five lawyers' work and that the marginal cost of serving another client approaches zero. Nori links this to increasingly affordable, open-source models and repetitive-task automation, drawing on his tenant-law practice and development of Roxanne the Repair Bot. Jeff Cox says tasks formerly taking hours can take minutes and predicts that AI's service benefits may eventually make non-use the ethical question. No common workload definition, controlled productivity comparison or full cost model accompanies these estimates.

pts.k: Legal Services NYC reports present operational benefits while deliberately withholding AI from direct client interactions.
pts.d: The report attributes to Alexander Horwitz current use of a private LLM for knowledge management, summaries and retrieval; finance automation reducing overtime; grant-reporting support; and analysis of poverty distributions and geographic legal need. It describes cautious discovery pilots, not wholesale automated legal representation. Horwitz's reservations concern hallucinations, explainability, quality control at hotline scale, and the loss of holistic human care. The hotline figures—approximately 120,000 annual calls and 60,000 answered—illustrate the service and monitoring burden rather than an AI impact estimate.

pts.k: Kristen Sonday presents existing legal-aid deployments as replicable examples of expanded reach and faster work.
pts.d: In July 2025 written testimony, Sonday describes Tennessee expungement automation producing draft petitions for attorney review and a clinic clearing 324 charges for 98 people in one day. She describes California Innocence Project use of CoCounsel to extract details and contradictions from large files; North Carolina's LIA legal-information assistant receiving over 95,000 views within months; and Housing Court Answers tools serving staff and tenants. She connects expungement assistance to housing and employment opportunities and document-review assistance to more time for case strategy. These are reported case examples: portal views are reach indicators, and no comparative legal-outcome study or quantified time baseline is supplied.

pts.k: Direct-to-public AI is presented as a route to unmet legal need, but speakers differ on acceptable delegation and timing.
pts.d: Nori argues that safeguarded, current legal AI should be publicly available because lawyer-only access entrenches exclusion; he advocates fundamental reform or abolition of existing UPL laws. Randal Jeffrey distinguishes internal assistance, external client interaction and freestanding services without attorney involvement. He envisages intake, status explanations, document production and potentially whole-matter handling, but explicitly frames much of this as unanswered questions, not demonstrated capability or a settled deployment recommendation. His courtroom-avatar example involved conveying an argument, not generating advocacy in real time. The Committee's adopted position is more incremental than Nori's: examine UPL barriers cautiously and postpone narrow client-facing tools until governance, training and evaluation are established.

pts.k: AI may personalize legal information, automate multi-step support and reduce software-development costs.
pts.d: Sam Harden offers prospective examples of agents retrieving case information, preparing medical-record requests for lawyer signature, and calendaring hearings from filings. These are plausible scenarios rather than reported deployments. He also describes AI-assisted rapid prototyping of decision-tree tools and predicts organizations may eventually substitute models for some development-firm work. His comparison of 2023 Bard with contemporary Gemini Deep Research illustrates perceived improvement in legal guidance: a 2024 survey rated the earlier response 3.11/5 for helpfulness and 3.56/5 for actionable next steps, whereas the newer response is assessed qualitatively. No equivalent scored evaluation of the newer response is presented.

pts.k: Reliability failures can harm clients at scale, and source grounding is not treated uniformly as a complete solution.
pts.d: Cox attributes reduced hallucination and confidentiality concerns to vLex's authoritative-source grounding, verification links and zero-retention agreements. His statements reflect his role at the vendor as well as his legal-aid board experience. Jeffrey expressly cautions that RAG does not guarantee quality, particularly for nuanced questions. Aubrie Souza and Zachary Zarnow warn that unrepresented users may not identify inaccurate, incomplete or irrelevant answers and that incorrect court-provided guidance can erode public trust. Harden emphasizes the speed, scale and potential unaccountability of confidently wrong outputs. Hedges invokes Mata and subsequent case law as warning examples, not as measured hallucination rates.

pts.k: AI could widen the justice gap through unequal organizational resources, digital exclusion and dependence on vendors.
pts.d: Colpoys, Cox and Sonday warn that commercial practitioners or better-funded legal-aid organizations may gain capabilities unavailable to resource-constrained nonprofits. Sonday calls for shared infrastructure and targeted investment; Colpoys describes training and funding support through the Lawyers Trust Fund of Illinois. Souza and Zarnow warn that apparently inexpensive services may become financially unsustainable as court reliance on third parties grows. The Committee also highlights internet access, language and disability barriers. Its discussion of disability-related bias is attributed to a separate New York City Bar task-force report, rather than to the NYSBA survey.

pts.k: Faster legal production is not necessarily beneficial throughout the justice system.
pts.d: The report attributes to Reents a warning that faster drafting and filing can increase court workloads faster than adjudicative capacity and that speed may disadvantage tenants where additional time is beneficial. The Committee also rejects interpreting efficiency gains as a justification for staffing cuts. Its account of client-facing limitations stresses that explicit legal questions can conceal childcare, transport, health or safety needs that skilled human intake workers identify.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines adoption surveys, practitioner and vendor testimony, reported deployments and policy authority; broad impact predictions are not established by a common outcome study.
pts.d: The principal New York survey contains 206 responses from 715 people contacted, a reported 28.8% response rate, distributed through NYSBA channels and organizational leadership. It measures self-reported familiarity, use, concerns and preferences, not causal effects on client outcomes. The separate Illinois October 2024 survey contains 376 responses and approximately 90% reporting no or slight work use; it should not be merged with the New York sample. The May 21, 2025 hearing and subsequent written testimony supply professional experience, examples and predictions. Sonday's clinic and portal figures are deployment evidence; Harden's ratings concern perceived response usefulness; none is a sector-wide productivity benchmark. The report cites the Legal Services Corporation's 2022 justice-gap findings as context for unmet need, not evidence that AI has reduced that gap. Court policies and annexed organizational policies provide governance authority rather than effectiveness measurements. The authors disclose Microsoft Copilot-assisted synthesis with human oversight. The report's unattributed reference to a solid first pass '90% of the time' is an experience-based characterization without an identified test protocol or named speaker in that passage.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report supplies a 2025 baseline and an open-ended, conditional adoption forecast, not a dated transformation timetable.
pts.d: The New York survey ran February 3–April 9, 2025; the hearing occurred May 21; Sonday's testimony is dated July; the Committee approved the report October 28, 2025; and the House of Delegates approved it January 16, 2026. Current operational examples and early-adoption findings should be distinguished from statements about what AI could or eventually will do. The adopted sequence requires policy, approved tools, training, source grounding, human verification, audit trails, data preparation and evaluation before client-facing expansion. Pilots receive proposed 30–60-day review dates, not promised benefit-realization deadlines. The Committee recommends baselines for hours saved, cycle times, errors, first-review acceptance and equity effects. Its safeguards are proposed conditions for responsible adoption, not a demonstrated guarantee of error-free performance. Nori's public-access urgency and Harden's encouragement of experimentation remain distinct from the Committee's more cautious institutional sequence.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are civil legal-aid providers, underserved individuals and courts, with secondary effects on education, funders and technology suppliers.
pts.d: Lawyers, paralegals, advocates and intake workers may gain capacity and shift toward judgment, advocacy and human care; finance, grants, data and technology staff may reduce administrative work. Low-income clients and self-represented people may obtain more timely, personalized, plain-language assistance, but face misinformation, privacy breaches, inadequate escalation and unequal access. Tenants, immigrants, people with disabilities, survivors of violence, debtors and rural or digitally excluded users receive particular attention. The Immigration Representation Committee's support memorandum emphasizes potential detention, removal and family-separation consequences from legal errors. Courts may improve information management and staff workflows while confronting more filings and public-trust risks. Funders influence whether shared infrastructure and training prevent two-tier adoption. Legal-tech vendors face demands for confidentiality, testing and accountability; development firms may face substitution for some prototyping work. Nori additionally argues that law schools must integrate AI literacy into core courses and clinics. The report does not offer a concrete forecast about law-firm staffing shapes, associate leverage or enterprise legal-market shares.
